q.e: Give 1 shock, then immediately resume CPR for about 2 minutes before reanalysis.

q.q: For a child under 8 years, which AED pads and dose should be used?
o: Child pads and the child dose; adult pads if child pads are unavailable
Adult pads and the adult dose; child pads only if adult pads are missing
No AED under 8 years; use manual defibrillation only
Child pads and the adult dose; adult pads are never used
q.e: < 8 years: child pads/child dose; adult pads may be used if child pads are unavailable (not overlapping).

q.q: What is the IV/IO epinephrine dose during cardiac arrest?
q.e: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO (10 mL of 1:10,000) every 3–5 minutes.

q.q: What is the first dose of amiodarone for refractory VF/pulseless VT?
q.e: Amiodarone 300 mg first, then 150 mg.

q.q: Which drugs can be given through the ETT (NAVEL)?
q.e: NAVEL; give 2–2.5× the IV dose diluted in 10 mL; IO is preferred today.

q.q: When is magnesium sulfate given during cardiac arrest?
o: For torsades de pointes or suspected low magnesium
For every arrest with ventricular fibrillation
For asystole after the second epinephrine dose
For hyperkalemia with peaked T waves
q.e: Magnesium 1–2 g only if torsades or suspected hypomagnesemia.

q.q: What is the most common IO site?
q.e: Deck: proximal tibia (also humerus); IO when IV access is too difficult.

q.q: During CPR, the PETCO₂ is 8 mm Hg. What does this indicate?
o: Poor pulmonary blood flow — improve CPR quality
Return of spontaneous circulation has occurred
Compressions are effective and should continue
Pulmonary blood flow is normal, so CPR needs no adjustment
q.e: PETCO₂ < 10 mm Hg = poor or absent pulmonary blood flow → improve CPR.

q.q: What PETCO₂ change suggests ROSC?
o: An abrupt, sustained increase, typically to about 40 mm Hg
A gradual fall toward zero over several minutes
A steady value that stays below 10 mm Hg
A brief rise that follows each ventilation and then returns to baseline
q.e: An abrupt, sustained rise (often ≥ 40 mm Hg) indicates ROSC.

q.q: After ROSC, what PETCO₂ target guides ventilation?
q.e: Post-arrest: start at 10 breaths/min and titrate to PETCO₂ 35–40 mm Hg.

q.q: How does the impedance threshold valve improve CPR?
o: It makes intrathoracic pressure more negative on recoil, raising venous return
It delivers extra oxygen during chest recoil, raising the arterial oxygen saturation
It removes CO₂ during compressions, lowering the arterial PCO₂
It raises intrathoracic pressure on recoil, raising coronary perfusion
q.e: The ITV limits air entry on recoil, lowering intrathoracic pressure 6–8 mm Hg and raising venous return.
q.src: Advanced airways during CPR, and the impedance threshold valve

q.q: Why is early intubation usually not necessary during in-hospital adult CPR?
o: Intubation in the first 15 minutes is associated with decreased survival
Intubation cannot be performed safely while chest compressions are in progress
Bag-mask ventilation gives a higher FiO₂ than an endotracheal tube
Compressions must stop for 2 minutes while the tube is placed
q.e: BVM allows uninterrupted compressions; early IHCA intubation is linked to lower survival.
q.src: Advanced airways during CPR, and the impedance threshold valve

q.q: Which advanced airway can be used with a possible unstable neck injury and needs no view of the cords?
q.e: The LMA is easy to insert without seeing the cords and can be used with possible neck injury.
q.src: Advanced airways during CPR, and the impedance threshold valve

q.q: What SpO₂ target does Hess give after ROSC?
q.e: Titrate FiO₂ to the minimum needed for SpO₂ 94%; avoid hyperoxia and hyperventilation.

q.q: After return of spontaneous circulation, a patient does not follow commands. Which of the following should be started?
o: Immediate extubation to a nasal cannula
Hyperventilation to a PaCO₂ of 25 mm Hg
q.e: Algorithm 18-8: if the patient does not follow commands after ROSC, initiate TTM.

q.q: Which is one of the 'T's' among the reversible causes of arrest?
q.e: T's: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, coronary thrombosis.

q.q: When do most post-resuscitation deaths occur?
q.e: Most post-resuscitation deaths occur in the first 24 hours.

q.q: An adult who is choking can't speak and nods when asked. What should be done?
o: Give back blows and chest thrusts
q.e: Severe obstruction in adults/children: abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts if pregnant or obese).
q.src: Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) by age

q.q: How is severe choking relieved in an infant?
o: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts, repeated
A blind finger sweep, then 2 breaths
5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated
q.e: Infants: no abdominal thrusts — 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.
q.src: Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) by age

q.q: A choking adult becomes unresponsive. Which of the following is the next step?
o: Lower to the ground, activate EMS and start CPR with no pulse check
Continue abdominal thrusts while holding the patient upright
Check the pulse for 10 seconds, then give 5 back blows
Place in the recovery position, give oxygen and wait for EMS to arrive
q.e: Start compressions (no pulse check), and look in the mouth each time the airway is opened.
q.src: Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) by age

q.q: Who can start CPR, and who can order it withheld?
o: Anyone may start CPR; withholding it requires a physician's order
A physician must order CPR; a nurse may order it withheld
Anyone may start CPR; the family may order it withheld
A physician must order CPR; anyone may decide to withhold it
q.e: CPR is started without an order (implied consent); withholding requires a physician's order.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: Infants and children usually arrest because of what?
q.e: Pediatric arrests are usually secondary to respiratory causes; adult arrests usually follow VF.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for coronary heart disease (Box 18-1)?
q.e: Smoking is the most important; CHD death rate is 70% greater in smokers.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: In newborn resuscitation, when are chest compressions started?
q.e: Algorithm 18-4: PPV if HR < 100, gasping or apnea; compressions if HR < 60 despite ventilation.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: The Heuer Ch 15 deck says CPR quality should be improved if the intra-arterial diastolic pressure is below what?
q.e: PetCO₂ < 10 mm Hg and/or arterial diastolic pressure < 20 mm Hg → improve CPR.
q.src: What Heuer Ch 15 adds or words differently

q.q: With an ETT in place, how often does the Heuer deck give breaths during CPR?
o: One every 6–8 seconds without pausing compressions
One every 2 seconds without pausing compressions
Two after every 30 compressions, with a pause
One every 20 seconds without pausing compressions
q.e: Heuer: 1 breath every 6–8 s; Hess: every 6 s (10/min).
q.src: What Heuer Ch 15 adds or words differently

q.q: Which drugs does the Heuer deck list as L-E-A-N for ETT instillation?
q.e: L-E-A-N; some add vasopressin to make N-A-V-E-L.
q.src: What Heuer Ch 15 adds or words differently

sections.title: Mechanical Ventilation
sections.covers: 30 items · Modes (VC, PC, IMV, MMV, SIMV, PRVC, CMV, PAV, APRV, HFOV, VV+) and asynchrony · variables · PEEP, dangerous levels, auto-PEEP · high and low pressures · trigger and cycle · independent vs dependent variables · circuits and exhalation valves · the equation of motion

q.q: Why do the decks say to 'learn how the mode works — not just the name'?
o: Mode names are not standardized between manufacturers
Mode names are fixed by an international standard
Mode names determine the alarm limits that apply
Mode names differ by patient age, not by maker
q.e: Names are manufacturer-dependent (e.g. PRVC on Servo = VC+ on PB840 = AutoFlow on Dräger).
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: According to the golden rule, how many variables can a ventilator control at once?
o: None — the patient controls each one
q.e: Control volume and pressure varies; control pressure and volume varies.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: A breath is triggered by the patient but cycled by the ventilator. How is it classified?
q.e: "If the patient controls both = Spontaneous. If the ventilator controls either one = it's Mandatory."
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: Which breath sequence consists of all spontaneous breaths, such as CPAP or PS?
q.e: CMV = all mandatory; IMV = mandatory plus spontaneous; CSV = all spontaneous.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: Which ventilatory pattern is NOT valid, according to Hess?
q.e: Presetting VT implies machine cycling, so volume control can't be continuous spontaneous ventilation.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: What is an open-loop ventilator?
o: One that delivers what you set and doesn't adjust, such as VC
One that adjusts its output automatically to the patient
One that leaves the exhalation valve open during inspiration
One that measures exhaled volume to correct the next breath
q.e: Open-loop delivers what is set (VC); closed-loop watches and adjusts (PSV, MMV, PRVC, PAV, NAVA).
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: In volume control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: VT stays the same and pressure increases
VT falls and pressure stays the same
q.e: VC guarantees VT; pressure is the dependent variable and rises as compliance falls.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: In pressure control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: Pressure stays the same and VT decreases
VT stays the same and pressure rises
Pressure falls and VT stays the same
q.e: PC guarantees pressure; VT falls with decreased compliance.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: PC is set at 20 cm H₂O with PEEP 10 cm H₂O. What is the PIP?
q.e: PIP = pressure control + PEEP = 20 + 10 = 30 cm H₂O.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: Which pressure waveform 'looks like a table' with a plateau?
q.e: PC: square pressure waveform with a plateau and descending flow; VC: "mountain" pressure with square flow.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: When does Hess say volume control should be used?
o: Whenever a constant VT is important to maintain a desired PaCO₂
Whenever a limit on peak alveolar pressure is the priority
Whenever the patient has a large and variable air leak
Whenever the patient's inspiratory flow demand varies
q.e: Hess: VC whenever a constant tidal volume is important for the desired PaCO₂.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: A patient on volume control needs a plateau pressure above 30 cm H₂O. Which of the following does the RCP 203 deck suggest?
o: Increase the VT to improve ventilation
Add more PEEP at the same VT
Switch to SIMV without pressure support
q.e: RCP 203: a patient needing Pplat > 30 in VC should probably be switched to PC at ≤ 30.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: What is the key difference between the control mode (CMV) and assist/control?
o: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; CMV (control) does not
CMV allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths; A/C does not
A/C has no set rate; CMV (control) has a set rate
CMV uses pressure support on triggered breaths; A/C does not
q.e: The slide's one-line difference: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; control mode does not.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: A/C is set at 12 breaths/min and the patient triggers 24. How many full breaths are delivered?
q.e: In A/C every triggered breath gets the full preset support; the set rate is a minimum.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: How is a patient-triggered (assisted) breath identified on the pressure waveform?
o: A negative deflection below baseline before inspiration
A positive spike just after exhalation ends
A flat baseline before the pressure rises
A sudden drop of the PEEP level to zero before inspiration
q.e: Assist = negative deflection before inspiration; time-triggered control breaths have none.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: What is a complication of A/C when the patient triggers at a high rate?
o: Hypoxemia from a falling delivered FiO₂
Atelectasis from a low mean airway pressure
q.e: High frequency in A/C → alveolar hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis) and possibly auto-PEEP.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: Which alarms are most important in the control mode?
o: Low exhaled volume and low inspiratory pressure
High PEEP/CPAP and high exhaled minute volume
q.e: In control mode, the most important alarms are low exhaled volume and low inspiratory pressure.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: What problem does IMV (unsynchronized) cause that SIMV avoids?
q.e: IMV can deliver a mandatory breath before a spontaneous one is exhaled → breath stacking, auto-PEEP.

q.q: SIMV is set at a rate of 10 and the patient breathes at 20. What does the patient receive?
o: 20 mandatory breaths and no spontaneous breaths
20 spontaneous breaths and no mandatory breaths
10 mandatory breaths and no spontaneous breaths
q.e: SIMV gives the set mandatory breaths; extra breaths are spontaneous (A/C would give 20 mandatory).

q.q: In SIMV with PS 8, which breaths receive the pressure support?
o: The spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths
The mandatory breaths that the patient triggers
All breaths, both mandatory and spontaneous
No breaths, since PS is inactive in SIMV
q.e: PS applies only to spontaneous breaths; mandatory breaths deliver the preset VT.

q.q: Why is SIMV usually combined with pressure support?
o: To prevent muscle fatigue and high WOB on spontaneous breaths
To increase the mandatory rate when the patient tires
To guarantee the set tidal volume on every spontaneous breath
To lower the FiO₂ needed during mandatory breaths
q.e: Without PS, SIMV can cause muscle fatigue and weaning failure; PS helps the spontaneous breaths.

q.q: How does the instructor's word-play list treat SIMV?
q.e: Word-play: "SIMV = IMV" — treat them as the same breath sequence unless the stem is about breath stacking.

q.q: How is pressure support classified?
q.e: PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — a phrase on NBRC-style exams repeatedly.

q.q: When does a pressure-supported breath end?
o: When inspiratory flow falls to a preset % of peak flow, often ~25%
When a fixed inspiratory time has passed since the trigger, often 1 second
When the preset tidal volume has been delivered
When airway pressure falls 2 cm H₂O below PEEP
q.e: PS breaths flow-cycle, often at about 25% of peak flow.

q.q: Why can PSV not be used alone in an apneic patient?
o: Every PS breath must be patient-triggered
Every PS breath delivers too large a volume
PS has no adjustable FiO₂ or PEEP setting
PS breaths are time-cycled, not flow-cycled
q.e: PS is active only on spontaneous breaths, so it needs an intact respiratory drive.

q.q: PS is set too high. What may Hess say happens?
o: Repeated apnea alarms with no other effect
A fall in the tidal volume
q.e: Too low → fatigue and tachypnea; too high → expiratory muscle activation.

q.q: How does MMV ensure adequate ventilation?
o: It increases mandatory breaths when spontaneous V̇E falls below a preset minimum
It guarantees the set VT on every spontaneous breath that is taken
It raises PEEP automatically when the measured SpO₂ falls below a preset minimum
It increases pressure support when the spontaneous rate rises too high
q.e: MMV is a "minimum ventilation safety net": low V̇E → more volume-cycled mandatory breaths.

q.q: On MMV with a target of 8 L/min, the patient breathes 9 L/min alone. What does the ventilator do?
q.e: If the patient breathes enough, MMV stays out of the way.

q.q: What does MMV NOT guarantee?
o: That every breath has an adequate VT
q.e: MMV guarantees minimum total V̇E, not an adequate VT on every breath.

q.q: Which mode automatically adjusts inspiratory pressure to maintain a target VT while minimizing airway pressure?
q.e: Board pearl: PRVC delivers the target VT at the lowest PIP possible.

q.q: On PRVC, the patient's compliance worsens. What does the ventilator do?
o: Raises the inspiratory pressure to deliver the target VT
Lowers the inspiratory pressure to protect the lungs
Keeps the pressure fixed and lets the VT fall
Switches to CPAP until the compliance improves
q.e: Compliance worsens → PRVC raises pressure; compliance improves → it lowers pressure.

q.q: On Automode, the patient makes two consecutive patient-triggered breaths. What happens?
o: It switches from PRVC to Volume Support
It switches from Volume Support to PRVC
It switches to apnea backup ventilation
It switches to CPAP with no support
q.e: Automode: sleeping patient → PRVC; awake patient (two triggered breaths) → Volume Support.

q.q: What is a caution about PRVC if a patient's demand rises inappropriately, e.g. from pain?
o: As VT rises, the ventilator lowers its pressure, which may be wrong for the patient
As VT rises, the ventilator raises its pressure to levels that can injure the lung
As VT rises, the ventilator stops all of the mandatory breaths
As VT rises, the ventilator raises the FiO₂ and the PEEP together
q.e: Hess: higher VT from pain makes PRVC lower its pressure, which may be inappropriate in respiratory failure.

q.q: What is Volume Control Plus (VC+) on the PB 840?
q.e: VC+ = PB's PRVC: preset VT and I-time with variable pressure and flow.

q.q: How does Volume Support differ from pressure support?
o: VS guarantees volume and lets pressure vary; PS fixes the pressure
VS is time-cycled and mandatory; PS is flow-cycled and spontaneous
VS needs a set rate and a set VT; PS needs a set rate alone
VS fixes the pressure and lets volume vary; PS guarantees volume
q.e: Both are patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled; VS targets volume.

q.q: On Volume Support, the patient makes more effort. What happens to the support pressure?
q.e: Less effort → higher PS; more effort → lower PS, to hold the target VT.

q.q: What does PAV target?
o: No set flow, volume or pressure; support is proportional to effort
A fixed tidal volume on every patient-triggered breath
A fixed inspiratory pressure above the PEEP level
A fixed minute ventilation with backup mandatory breaths as needed
q.e: "With PAV there is no target flow, volume, or pressure"; pull harder → more assist.

q.q: What happens if the PAV % assist is set too high?
o: Apnea with loss of the backup rate and low pressure
q.e: Too high → runaway; too low → excessive patient WOB.

q.q: Which patient is NOT suitable for PAV?
o: An apneic patient with no respiratory drive
A COPD patient who is being weaned
A patient who is coming off sedation
A patient with a variable respiratory drive
q.e: PAV requires intact drive and a functional neuromuscular system.

q.q: In PAV, what does 'flow assist' overcome?
q.e: Flow assist overcomes resistance; volume assist overcomes elastance.

q.q: How does the RCP 202 deck define APRV?
o: Inverse ratio, pressure-controlled IMV with unrestricted spontaneous breathing
Volume-controlled CMV with high rates, deep sedation and no spontaneous breathing
High-frequency oscillation around a constant mean airway pressure
Pressure support with a backup rate and a volume guarantee
q.e: APRV: inverse ratio, pressure-controlled, intermittent mandatory ventilation with unrestricted spontaneous breathing.

q.q: Which settings are used in APRV?
o: FiO₂, Phigh, Plow, Thigh and Tlow
Amplitude, Hz and mean airway pressure
q.e: APRV has no VT or rate setting; Thigh and Tlow set the release frequency.

q.q: How long does an adult spend at Plow during APRV (Hess)?
q.e: Tlow 0.2–0.8 s; 80–95% of the cycle is at Phigh, producing intrinsic PEEP.

q.q: How is APRV weaned in the Chang weaning deck?
o: Decrease the release frequency until the patient is essentially on CPAP
Raise Plow in steps until it equals Phigh
Increase the release frequency until Thigh is 1 second, then switch to SIMV
Switch to HFOV and lower the mean airway pressure
q.e: Decrease release frequency; at zero the patient is essentially on CPAP.

q.q: Which patient best fits APRV?
o: Hypoxemic failure/ARDS with an intact respiratory drive
An apneic, paralyzed patient with ARDS
A patient who needs a guaranteed tidal volume and a fixed PaCO₂
A COPD patient with severe air trapping
q.e: Classic APRV patient: significant hypoxemic failure with intact drive (not deeply paralyzed).

q.q: On HFOV, how is CO₂ removal improved?
o: Increase the amplitude or decrease the frequency (Hz)
Decrease the amplitude or increase the frequency (Hz)
Increase the mean airway pressure or the FiO₂
Decrease the bias flow or the inspiratory time %
q.e: ↓ Hz → larger oscillatory VT → ↑ CO₂ removal — "backwards from conventional ventilation."

q.q: On HFOV, how is oxygenation improved?
o: Increase the mean airway pressure or FiO₂
Decrease the mean airway pressure or bias flow
q.e: Oxygenation: ↑ mean airway pressure or ↑ FiO₂.

q.q: How does HFOV exhalation differ from conventional ventilation?
o: Exhalation is active — the oscillator pulls gas out
Exhalation is passive — elastic recoil pushes gas out
Exhalation is absent — gas leaves by diffusion alone
Exhalation is time-cycled — a valve opens at 1 Hz
q.e: HFOV actively pushes gas in and pulls it out; conventional exhalation is passive.

q.q: Is HFOV recommended routinely for adults with ARDS?
o: No — it has not shown benefit and may cause harm
Yes — it is first-line for moderate and severe ARDS
Yes — but only when the PEEP is above 20 cm H₂O
No — it is approved for neonates and children only
q.e: Trauma deck and Hess: not routinely recommended in adult ARDS; strong recommendation against routine use.

q.q: Which mode is described as 'tiny VT + very fast RR', with VT near or below dead space?
q.e: HFOV: extremely small volumes at 3–15 Hz (180–900 breaths/min).

q.q: Which mode gives a target VT at the lowest PIP with pressure auto-adjusted breath to breath?
q.e: Side-by-side table: PRVC = target VT at lowest PIP, pressure auto-adjusted.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: Which mode is listed as historical and not offered on new adult ventilators?
q.e: IMV causes breath stacking; all current ventilators offer SIMV instead.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: What is patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: The ventilator's breath delivery is out of phase with the patient's effort
The patient's heart rate is out of phase with the breaths that are being delivered
The ventilator's alarm limits do not match the patient's values
The set FiO₂ does not match the oxygen analyzer reading
q.e: Hess: synchrony = breath delivery in phase with patient effort; asynchrony = out of phase.

q.q: Which is a consequence of patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: Increased WOB and sedation needs, and longer ventilation
Lower oxygen cost of breathing, less sedation and shorter ventilation
Shorter weaning time and less muscle fatigue
Improved comfort and a lower respiratory rate
q.e: Asynchrony decreases comfort, increases WOB and sedation needs, and prolongs ventilation.

q.q: A COPD patient's observed respiratory rate is higher than the rate the ventilator displays. Which of the following is the likely cause?
o: Auto-PEEP preventing some efforts from triggering
A trigger that is set too sensitive for the patient's effort
A leak in the ventilator circuit
q.e: Patient rate > ventilator rate means efforts are missed, commonly from auto-PEEP raising the trigger threshold.

q.q: What is the usual pressure-trigger setting?
q.e: Hess: set so trigger effort is minimal but auto-triggering unlikely — 1–2 cm H₂O below PEEP.

q.q: The ventilator delivers breaths although the patient is making no visible effort. What should you think of first?
o: Flow starvation from a low flow
q.e: "Think leak" when breaths appear in a patient making no obvious efforts; water and cardiac oscillations also auto-trigger.

q.q: A trigger is changed from −3 to −1 cm H₂O. What has happened?
q.e: Closer to zero = more sensitive; farther from zero (−5) = less sensitive.

q.q: During VC, a vigorous patient effort pulls the pressure waveform downward and PIP varies breath to breath. What is the problem?
q.e: The ventilator isn't meeting inspiratory flow demand; fix by raising flow or switching to PC/PS.

q.q: A pressure dip early in inspiration on the waveform suggests what?
o: Inadequate peak flow — 'I need more flow'
Too much tidal volume — 'I need less volume'
Delayed cycling — 'I want to exhale now'
A circuit leak — 'the breath is escaping'
q.e: Early dip = "I need more flow"; late dip = "I want more volume."

q.q: The ventilator ends inspiration while the patient's inspiratory effort continues, and that same effort immediately triggers a second breath, nearly doubling the set VT. What is this?
q.e: Premature cycling: the patient's effort continues after the breath ends and double-triggers.

q.q: On PS in a COPD patient, a pressure spike appears at end-inspiration and the abdomen tightens. What is happening?
o: Delayed cycling — the patient is actively exhaling against the breath
Premature cycling — the breath ends before the patient's effort stops
Flow starvation — the patient is pulling against a low set flow
Auto-triggering — the ventilator is responding to a circuit leak
q.e: In obstruction, flow decays slowly and never reaches the cycle threshold; the patient fights to exhale.

q.q: How can delayed cycling on PS be fixed?
o: Lower the PS level or raise the termination-flow (cycle) setting
Raise the PS level or lower the termination-flow (cycle) setting
Make the trigger less sensitive and lengthen the rise time
Increase the PEEP and shorten the expiratory time
q.e: Hess: lower PS, raise the cycle percentage, or switch to time-cycled PC.

q.q: What is the recommended order for fixing asynchrony?
o: Adjust settings → reconsider the mode → sedation/analgesia → neuromuscular blockade last
Neuromuscular blockade → sedation/analgesia → adjust settings → change the mode
Reconsider the mode → neuromuscular blockade → adjust settings → sedation
Sedation/analgesia → neuromuscular blockade → reconsider the mode → settings
q.e: Troubleshoot and adjust settings first; "Paralytics don't fix problems — they hide them."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What does Hess call a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator?
q.e: "Anxiety is a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: Why can SIMV itself cause mode asynchrony?
o: The respiratory center cannot adapt to the varying breath types
The mandatory breaths are never synchronized with the patient's effort
The spontaneous breaths are larger than the mandatory breaths
The pressure support is active on the mandatory breaths alone
q.e: Mode asynchrony occurs when the ventilator delivers different breath types, as in SIMV.
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: Before using a paralytic for asynchrony, what must be done?
o: Troubleshoot: kinked tube, secretions, wrong settings, circuit issues
Increase sedation before checking the airway and ventilator settings
Change the ventilator mode before inspecting the tube and circuit
Switch to CPAP and allow the PaCO₂ to rise
q.e: NMBA deck: "DO NOT jump to paralytics"; paralysis always requires ventilation plus sedation.
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What does Automatic Tube Compensation (ATC) do?
o: Offsets the tube's resistance so breathing feels as if the tube weren't there
Guarantees a minimum minute ventilation by adding mandatory breaths when needed
Raises the PEEP automatically when the endotracheal tube narrows
Clears secretions from the tube by reversing the inspiratory flow
q.e: ATC compensates during inspiration and expiration; a smaller ETT needs more compensation.

q.q: What I:E ratio does inverse ratio ventilation use?
q.e: Normal I:E is 1:1.5 to 1:3; IRV uses 2:1 to 4:1 to raise mean airway pressure.

q.q: Which is an adverse effect of inverse ratio ventilation?
o: Auto-PEEP from the short expiratory time
Lower mean airway pressure and atelectasis
Improved venous return and cardiac output
Less need for sedation and paralysis
q.e: IRV: ↓ venous return, auto-PEEP, barotrauma, dyssynchrony needing more sedation.

q.q: What does ASV (Adaptive Support Ventilation) target?
o: A minute ventilation, choosing rate and VT for the lowest WOB
A fixed peak pressure, choosing the tidal volume for each breath
A fixed tidal volume, choosing the lowest possible rate
A fixed I:E ratio of 4:1, choosing the rate for comfort
q.e: ASV targets V̇E (via IBW) and uses the Otis equation to pick the rate with the lowest WOB.

q.q: What is normal adult inspiratory flow per the Principles deck?
q.e: Principles deck: normal adult inspiratory flow = 40–60 L/min.

q.q: With constant flow of 60 L/min for 1 second, what tidal volume is delivered?
q.e: 60 L/min = 1 L/s; VT = flow × TI = 1 L.

q.q: What are the three control variables per the Principles deck?
q.e: Control variables: volume, pressure and time; trigger/limit/cycle are phase variables.

q.q: PEEP is 5 cm H₂O and PIP is 25 cm H₂O. What pressure drives inspiration above baseline?
q.e: Measured from baseline: 25 − 5 = 20 cm H₂O.

q.q: What is the 'independent variable' on a ventilator?
o: Whatever the alarm limit is set to
q.e: "Whatever the ventilator guarantees is called the independent variable"; the other floats.

q.q: In PC, which change increases the delivered VT?
o: More auto-PEEP at the same PIP
Lower compliance at the same PIP
Higher airway resistance at the same PIP
q.e: Box 20-5: VT rises with ↑ driving pressure, longer TI (while flow present) and more effort.

q.q: In VC, which change raises PIP?
q.e: Box 20-4: PIP rises with ↑ flow, constant flow, ↑ PEEP, auto-PEEP, ↑ VT, ↑ Raw, ↓ compliance.

q.q: In VC, airway resistance increases. What happens to PIP − Pplat?
o: It increases, while Pplat is unchanged
It decreases, while Pplat is unchanged
It stays the same, while Pplat rises
It decreases, while Pplat also falls
q.e: ↑ Raw in VC: ↑ PIP, ↑ PIP − Pplat, no change in Pplat.

q.q: What starts a time-triggered breath?
q.e: Rate 12 → a breath every 5 s; time-triggered breaths show no negative deflection.

q.q: Base flow is 10 L/min and flow sensitivity is 3 L/min. When does the ventilator trigger?
o: When expiratory-circuit flow drops to 7 L/min
When expiratory-circuit flow rises to 13 L/min
When expiratory-circuit flow drops to 3 L/min
When expiratory-circuit flow drops to zero
q.e: Hess's example: it triggers at 7 L/min, assuming the patient inhaled 3 L/min.

q.q: A trigger set at −5 cm H₂O is too insensitive. What results?
o: The patient may not be able to trigger and fatigues
The ventilator auto-triggers from small leaks or cardiac motion
The ventilator double-triggers on each effort
The ventilator delivers an excessive VT
q.e: Too high (not sensitive enough) → can't trigger; too sensitive (−0.5) → auto-trigger.

q.q: Why can auto-PEEP make triggering difficult?
o: It is a threshold pressure the patient must overcome before triggering
It lowers the baseline pressure so that the trigger is reached too soon
It increases the flow sensitivity so that small leaks trigger breaths
It closes the exhalation valve so that the trigger cannot be sensed
q.e: Neither pressure nor flow triggering may be effective with significant auto-PEEP.

q.q: According to the deck's memory line, how is pressure control cycled?
q.e: "Volume Control is volume-cycled. Pressure Control is time-cycled. PSV is flow-cycled."

q.q: When does pressure cycling most often occur?
o: As an alarm condition when the high-pressure limit is reached
On every pressure-supported breath as flow decays
On every volume-controlled breath at end-inspiration
On every oscillation during high-frequency oscillatory ventilation
q.e: Pressure cycling most often occurs as a high-pressure alarm condition (e.g. a cough during VC).

q.q: How is Volume Support classified (trigger/limit/cycle)?
q.e: VS: patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — like PS but volume-targeted.

q.q: What is the number one ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation?
q.e: Pearl: PEEP is primarily an oxygenation intervention, not a ventilation intervention.

q.q: How does PEEP improve oxygenation?
o: It keeps alveoli open at end-expiration, raising FRC and reducing shunt
It increases the respiratory rate, raising the minute ventilation and the PaO₂
It removes CO₂ at end-expiration, raising the alveolar PO₂
It lowers the FRC at end-expiration, reducing dead space
q.e: PEEP prevents end-expiratory collapse → ↑ FRC → ↑ V/Q → better oxygenation.

q.q: What is CPAP?
o: PEEP applied to a patient breathing entirely on their own
A mandatory mode with a set rate and pressure
Pressure support with a backup rate
PEEP applied only during the mandatory breaths of a control mode
q.e: CPAP = PEEP with all spontaneous breaths; on BiPAP, EPAP = PEEP.

q.q: What initial PEEP does the Initiation deck give for refractory hypoxemia?
q.e: Start at 5 cm H₂O ("NBRC range 2–6"), then adjust by FiO₂ need and cardiovascular response.

q.q: How is 'optimal PEEP' defined in the Management of MV deck?
o: The lowest pressure that offers the most benefit with the least side effects
The highest pressure that the patient can tolerate before hypotension develops
The pressure of 10 cm H₂O that is used for all adult patients
The lowest pressure that gives a PaO₂ above 150 mm Hg
q.e: Titrate with PaO₂, compliance, saturation and waveforms; e.g. 10 is optimal if 12 lowers PaO₂ and compliance.

q.q: Where should PEEP be set on a pressure–volume loop?
o: Just above the lower inflection point
Just above the upper inflection point
Just below the lower inflection point
Midway between zero and the lower inflection point
q.e: Answer "just above the LIP" (deck: at/slightly above; RCP 203: 2–3 cm H₂O above).

q.q: What PEEP level does the RCP 202 slide associate with an increased incidence of barotrauma?
q.e: "PEEP > 10 (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50) is associated with increased alveolar rupture or barotrauma."

q.q: What is the major downside of PEEP?
o: Decreased venous return, cardiac output and blood pressure
Increased venous return, preload, cardiac output and blood pressure
Hypercapnia from a lower respiratory rate
q.e: ↑ PEEP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP.

q.q: How can PEEP raise ICP?
o: Higher intrathoracic pressure impedes venous drainage from the brain
Lower intrathoracic pressure increases arterial flow to the brain
It dilates the cerebral arteries by raising the PaO₂
It increases CSF production by raising the cardiac output
q.e: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, impeding cerebral venous drainage.

q.q: With PPV and PEEP, why can CVP rise while preload actually falls?
o: Intrathoracic pressure raises the measured CVP even as venous return decreases
The measured CVP always equals preload, so both of them must rise
PEEP increases the circulating blood volume as venous return rises
The catheter tip migrates into the right ventricle each time the lungs are inflated
q.e: "High CVP does not always mean lots of preload."

q.q: What is auto-PEEP?
o: Unintentional PEEP from gas trapped when exhalation is incomplete
Intentional PEEP set by the clinician to improve oxygenation
Unintentional PEEP caused by a leak in the circuit or cuff
Intentional PEEP added by the ventilator after an apnea alarm
q.e: Auto-PEEP (intrinsic, inadvertent, occult PEEP) = trapped gas; total PEEP = set PEEP + auto-PEEP.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP detected on the flow–time waveform?
o: Expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath
Inspiratory flow has a square shape instead of a ramp
Expiratory flow returns to zero early, followed by a long pause at baseline
Inspiratory flow starts with a negative deflection
q.e: Expiratory flow failing to reach baseline before the next breath = air trapping.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP measured?
o: An end-expiratory pause; pause pressure minus set PEEP
An end-inspiratory pause; plateau pressure minus set PEEP
No pause; peak pressure minus plateau pressure
An end-expiratory pause; exhaled VT minus set VT
q.e: Occlude just before the next breath; e.g. 12 − 5 = 7 cm H₂O auto-PEEP. The patient must be relaxed.

q.q: Which ventilator change reduces auto-PEEP?
o: Decrease the respiratory rate to lengthen expiratory time
Increase the respiratory rate to raise minute ventilation
Decrease the inspiratory flow to lengthen inspiratory time
Increase the tidal volume to improve lung emptying
q.e: Give the lungs more time to empty: ↓ rate, ↑ flow, ↓ VT, bronchodilators.

q.q: A COPD patient on a rate of 20, VT 700 mL and flow 40 L/min develops rising PIP, auto-PEEP and hypotension. Which of the following should be done?
o: Lower VT and rate, increase flow, and lengthen expiratory time
Raise the VT to 900 mL and keep the same rate and the same flow
Raise the rate to 30 and shorten the expiratory time
Lower the flow to 20 L/min and lengthen inspiration
q.e: Principles deck vignette: lower VT, lower RR, increase flow, increase expiratory time.

q.q: In volume control, how does auto-PEEP affect PIP?
o: It changes only the plateau pressure
q.e: In VC auto-PEEP raises PIP; in PC it reduces VT.

q.q: When should applied (therapeutic) PEEP be used to counter auto-PEEP?
o: After ventilator adjustments, mainly to help triggering in obstructive disease
Before any other ventilator adjustment, in all types of lung disease
During paralysis, mainly to raise the functional residual capacity
After extubation, mainly to prevent the air trapping from returning during sleep
q.e: "Therapeutic PEEP should be used after making ventilator adjustments"; Hess: up to 75–85% of auto-PEEP.

q.q: What does PIP overcome, compared with plateau pressure?
o: PIP overcomes resistance and compliance; Pplat overcomes compliance only
PIP overcomes compliance only; Pplat overcomes resistance and compliance
PIP overcomes resistance only; Pplat overcomes resistance and compliance
PIP and Pplat both overcome resistance and compliance equally
q.e: Pplat is measured with no flow, so it excludes airway resistance; PIP − Pplat = flow × resistance.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: PIP rises from 25 to 40 cm H₂O while Pplat stays at 20. What is the likely cause?
o: Increased airway resistance, such as secretions or bronchospasm
Decreased lung compliance, such as ARDS or pulmonary edema
A tension pneumothorax or a main-stem intubation
Lobar atelectasis or a large pleural effusion
q.e: "When only PIP moves, think airways."
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: PIP and Pplat both rise by 10 cm H₂O. What is the likely cause?
o: Decreased compliance, such as pulmonary edema or pneumothorax
A mucus plug in the endotracheal tube or bronchospasm
The patient biting the tube or a kinked endotracheal tube
Water in the circuit or a blocked inspiratory filter
q.e: "When PIP and Plateau move together, think lungs."
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: Where should the high-pressure alarm be set (Initiation deck)?
o: 10 to 15 cm H₂O above the observed PIP
Equal to the observed peak pressure
5 to 10 cm H₂O below the observed PIP
25 to 30 cm H₂O above the observed PIP
q.e: High-pressure alarm: 10–15 cm H₂O above observed PIP; don't raise it without justification.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: What plateau pressure target should be used on this exam?
q.e: "Today, the accepted goal is a Pplat below 30 cm H₂O whenever possible."
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: How is driving pressure correctly calculated for the exam?
o: Pplat − PEEP, with a target < 15 cm H₂O
PIP − Pplat, with a target < 15 cm H₂O
PIP − PEEP, with a target < 30 cm H₂O
Pplat − PIP, with a target < 5 cm H₂O
q.e: True driving pressure = Pplat − PEEP (< 15); PIP − PEEP is total pressure including resistance.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: PIP 43, Pplat 40, flow 0.33 L/s. What is the airway resistance?
q.e: Raw = (PIP − Pplat) ÷ flow = 3 ÷ 0.33 ≈ 9.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: Which alarm in pressure control or pressure support detects changes in resistance and compliance (Hess)?
q.e: In VC the peak-pressure alarm detects changes; in PC or PS it is the low exhaled volume alarm.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: Where is the low inspiratory pressure alarm set?
o: 10 to 15 cm H₂O below the observed PIP
Equal to the set PEEP level
5 to 10 cm H₂O above the observed PIP
25 to 30 cm H₂O below the observed PIP
q.e: Low-pressure alarm: 10–15 below PIP, to detect leaks or disconnection.

q.q: According to Hess, what is the most important ventilator alarm?
q.e: Hess: the patient-disconnect alarm — a low-pressure and/or low exhaled volume alarm.

q.q: Expired VT is lower than set VT on every breath and PIP is lower than before. What is the problem?
q.e: A leak is low on every breath; with air trapping, expired VT is low for 2–3 breaths, then high.

q.q: The low PEEP alarm sounds. What is the usual cause?
o: A leak in the circuit or ETT cuff
q.e: "Failure of the circuit to hold PEEP is usually due to leakage in the circuit or ETT cuff."

q.q: An end-inspiratory squeak is heard over the trachea. What does it usually mean?
o: Insufficient air in the artificial airway cuff
Secretions pooled above the artificial airway cuff
A kink in the ventilator circuit
q.e: Hess: an end-inspiratory squeak usually means insufficient cuff air.

q.q: What delay is used for the apnea alarm?
q.e: Apnea alarm: 15–20 s delay; causes include disconnection, oversedation, neuromuscular block.

q.q: What is the correct response to a ventilator alarm?
o: Look at the patient, then the ventilator, find the cause and fix it
Silence the alarm, then check the chart and the orders for the cause
Widen the alarm limit, then reassess in 15 minutes
Check the ventilator first, then look at the patient
q.e: Alarm → patient → ventilator → cause → fix. Never silence an alarm and walk away.

q.q: Which circuit type is used on noninvasive ventilators?
o: Single-limb without an exhalation valve (a leak port)
Double-limb with a wye and an active exhalation valve
Single-limb with a mushroom exhalation valve at the patient
Double-limb with a leak port in the expiratory limb
q.e: NIV uses a known leak port; the ventilator calculates and subtracts the leak.

q.q: Where is the exhalation valve in a double-limb (wye) ICU circuit?
q.e: Double-limb circuits carry exhaled gas back to the ventilator's expiratory/PEEP valve.

q.q: Circuit compliance is 3 mL/cm H₂O, PIP 60 and PEEP 10. How much volume is compressed in the circuit?
q.e: 3 mL/cm H₂O × (60 − 10) = 150 mL; corrected VT = expired VT − 150 mL.

q.q: What is the most common threat to ventilator circuit patency?
q.e: Condensation from temperature drop increases resistance; manage with heated wires, water traps or an HME.

q.q: How often should ventilator circuits be changed for infection control?
o: Not routinely; change when visibly soiled
Every 8 hours, at each shift change
Every 48 hours, together with the humidifier chamber
q.e: Don't change routinely; weekly has been shown optimal; change when visibly soiled.

q.q: Adding an HME between the wye and the patient does what in a dual-limb circuit?
o: Has no effect on dead space
q.e: Any device between the wye and the airway adds mechanical dead space.

q.q: What are the two jobs of the exhalation valve?
o: Separate inspiration from expiration and set PEEP
Humidify the inspired gas and filter out bacteria
Measure the FiO₂ and trigger breaths
Warm the gas and measure the VT
q.e: Closed in inspiration, open for exhalation; the expiratory valve controls PEEP.

q.q: Which circuit obstruction is the more serious?
o: Expiratory — it can cause rebreathing, asphyxia or barotrauma
Inspiratory — it can prevent delivery of the prescribed tidal volume
Humidifier — it can cause overheating of the inspired gas
Inspiratory filter — it can restrict delivery of the set breath
q.e: Expiratory obstruction is more serious; it comes with low-volume and high-pressure alarms.

q.q: Why must the expiratory valve be checked during aerosolized ribavirin?
o: Ribavirin can crystallize and occlude valves and sensors
Ribavirin can raise the delivered FiO₂ and the PEEP
Ribavirin can dissolve the plastic of the circuit
Ribavirin can cause auto-triggering and stacking
q.e: Ribavirin crystals impair expiratory valves and sensors; watch for ↑ peak pressures.

q.q: What does the equation of motion describe?
o: The pressure needed to overcome airway resistance and lung/chest-wall elastance
The relationship between the inspired oxygen fraction and the arterial PO₂
The volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute during a breath
The amount of oxygen carried by hemoglobin and dissolved in plasma
q.e: Pressure must overcome R × flow (resistive load) and E × volume (elastic load).

q.q: In the equation of motion, what is elastance?
q.e: E = respiratory system elastance (lungs + chest wall), the inverse of compliance.

q.q: During full ventilatory support, what is Pmus in the equation of motion?
o: Zero — all pressure comes from the ventilator
Equal to the airway pressure the ventilator displays
q.e: Full support: Pmus = 0. Spontaneous breathing: Paw = 0. Partial: both contribute.

q.q: In ARDS, which term of the equation of motion rises?
q.e: ARDS: low compliance raises the elastic term; asthma raises the resistive term.

q.q: What VT and PEEP does the deck recommend during surgery?
o: VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW with low levels of PEEP
VT 12 mL/kg PBW with no PEEP
VT 4 mL/kg PBW with PEEP of 20
VT 10 mL/kg PBW with PEEP of 15 cm H₂O or more
q.e: Intraoperative lung-protective settings: VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW, low PEEP, Pplat < 30.

q.q: Which surgeries carry a 20–70% pulmonary complication rate?
q.e: Incision site matters: upper abdominal and thoracic surgery carry 20–70% complication rates.

q.q: What does the revised Key Point say about incentive spirometry after surgery?
o: Evidence does not support routine IS alone to prevent pulmonary complications
Evidence shows that routine IS alone prevents most pulmonary complications
Evidence shows that IS is contraindicated after abdominal surgery
Evidence supports IS as a replacement for early ambulation
q.e: Revised slide: evidence does not support routine IS alone; IS, PEP, CPAP still treat atelectasis.

q.q: A home patient on pressure control develops a mucus plug in the trach. Why might the high-pressure alarm stay silent?
o: The ventilator still reaches its set pressure while delivered VT falls
The plug lowers the airway pressure so that it stays below the alarm limit
Home ventilators have no high-pressure alarm to sound
The plug raises the delivered VT instead of the pressure
q.e: In PC, obstruction lowers VT but pressure is still reached; the low exhaled VT/minute volume alarm sounds instead.

q.q: How does exhaled gas leave a passive home ventilator circuit?
o: Through an intentional leak port that flushes exhaled CO₂
Through an active exhalation valve at the ventilator
Through the heated humidifier and its water trap
Back through the inspiratory limb, to be rebreathed
q.e: Passive circuits use a leak port (risk of CO₂ rebreathing if the leak is wrong); active circuits use a valve.

q.q: What must ventilator-dependent home patients and caregivers do before discharge?
o: Demonstrate competency in operation, airway care, alarms and emergency ventilation
Watch a training video on the ventilator, the humidifier, the alarms and the suction unit
Sign a consent form listing the equipment supplier
Arrange for home health staff to handle every alarm
q.e: They must demonstrate competency, not just hear about it; a resuscitation bag and backup power are needed.

sections.title: Noninvasive Support (NIPPV and HFNC)
sections.covers: 14 items · Describe Vapotherm · asynchrony on NIPPV · guideline and goals · cardiogenic pulmonary edema · MAP range · leak ports · PEEP vs PAP vs pharyngeal pressure

q.q: On this exam, what does 'Vapotherm' mean?
o: An ordinary nasal cannula running at 15 L/min
A non-rebreather mask with a reservoir bag
A heated aerosol by face tent or trach collar
q.e: Word-play: "HFNC = VapoTherm or Optiflow (NOT HFNC up to 15L)."

q.q: Why is a conventional nasal cannula limited to about 6–8 L/min?
o: Higher flows are uncomfortable without heated humidification
Higher flows deliver a toxic concentration of oxygen
The flowmeter and tubing cannot deliver more flow
Higher flows entrain more room air and so lower the delivered FiO₂
q.e: Heated humidification makes high flows comfortable; HFNC delivers up to 60 L/min.

q.q: What is the full FiO₂ range that HFNC can deliver, set independently of the flow?
q.e: The air/O₂ blender sets FiO₂ 0.21–1.0 independently of the flow.

q.q: What flow range does the RCP 203 deck give for adult HFNC?
q.e: Adults 1–40+ L/min, children 1–20 L/min, infants 1–8 L/min.

q.q: When setting up an older HFNC unit, what does the deck say to connect first?
o: The nasal cannula to the patient
q.e: "ALWAYS connect O₂ 'First'"; plug in the humidifier last and let it warm before connecting the cannula.

q.q: How does HFNC produce a modest CPAP effect?
o: Pharyngeal pressure rises ~1 cm H₂O per 10 L/min with the mouth closed
The prongs seal the nostrils and an exhalation valve holds the pressure
The device cycles between two pressures like a bilevel ventilator
Pharyngeal pressure is set on the machine at 5 to 10 cm H₂O
q.e: The flow opposes exhalation; the effect is lost if the patient opens their mouth.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: What is the most common indication for HFNC?
o: Status asthmaticus with a rising PaCO₂
q.e: HFNC decreases the intubation rate compared with conventional O₂ in acute hypoxemic failure.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: How is the ROX index calculated?
q.e: ROX = (SpO₂/FiO₂) ÷ RR; ≥ 4.88 predicts success, < 3.85 consider intubation.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: SpO₂ 92% on FiO₂ 0.50 with a rate of 20. What is the ROX index and what does it predict?
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: How does HFNC reduce the work of breathing?
o: By flushing anatomic dead space and lowering upper-airway resistance
By sealing the airway and applying a set level of PEEP on every breath
By delivering mandatory breaths at a set backup rate
By raising upper-airway resistance to slow the breathing
q.e: Dead-space washout and reduced upper-airway resistance lower WOB; a lower RR is common.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: What is the central cause of patient–ventilator asynchrony on NIV?
q.e: Leaks cause missed triggers, auto-triggering and delayed cycling.

q.q: On the V60, what does a total leak reading of '---' or '0' mean?
q.e: Normal total leak is 7–25; never over 60; '---' or '0' = mask too tight.

q.q: How can cycle asynchrony from a leak on NIV be improved?
o: Use time-cycled pressure control instead of flow-cycled pressure support
Use flow-cycled pressure support with a lower cycle % and a longer rise time
Lower the EPAP to zero and remove the backup rate
Switch to a nasal mask and raise the inspiratory pressure
q.e: Box 21-3: minimize leak, use time-cycled PC, adjust the flow-cycle setting, reduce PS.

q.q: A patient on NIV pressure support develops periods of apnea at night. Which of the following should be added?
q.e: PS has no backup rate; a backup rate is recommended, especially at night.

q.q: How should the rise time be set on BiPAP?
o: According to the patient's work of breathing, matching their effort
According to the backup rate, so each breath has the same shape
At the fastest setting for every patient, to shorten inspiration
At the slowest setting for every patient, to improve comfort
q.e: Rise is "set according to the pts WOB"; I-time is set according to the backup rate.

q.q: For which condition SHOULD NIV be used per the ERS/ATS guideline (CPG 21-2)?
q.e: NIV should be used: COPD exacerbation, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, postop failure, chest trauma, high-risk post-extubation prevention.

q.q: Which patient is excluded from NIV?
o: A patient with copious secretions and high aspiration risk
A COPD patient with a pH of 7.30 and a PaCO₂ of 60 mm Hg who is alert
A patient with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema
A patient with RR 28 and accessory-muscle use
q.e: Exclusions: airway protection problems (arrest, instability, aspiration risk, copious secretions), mask fit problems, uncooperative patient.

q.q: Which finding suggests a patient needs ventilatory support (step 1 of NIV selection)?
q.e: Box 21-1: respiratory distress, pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 45, RR > 25, or a diagnosis known to respond.

q.q: Which pH does the RCP 203 Ch 11 deck list as a contraindication to NIV?
q.e: RCP 203 contraindications include pH < 7.20, upper airway obstruction, uncontrolled arrhythmias, GI bleeding.

q.q: What is the primary goal of BiPAP, per the deck notes?
o: To reverse acute respiratory failure without an artificial airway
To cure the underlying disease before an artificial airway becomes necessary
To sedate the patient and lower the oxygen consumption
To raise the PaCO₂ and stimulate the respiratory drive
q.e: NIV will not cure the disease; it supports the patient until the disease is treated.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: A patient on NIV continues to deteriorate. When does the RCP 105 deck say to intubate?
o: If deteriorating 30 minutes after starting NIV
If no better 24 hours after starting NIV
If no better 4 hours after starting NIV
If deteriorating 5 minutes after starting NIV
q.e: Use the deck's 30 minutes; Hess says 1–2 hours.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: Why may NPPV be chosen over intubation?
o: It preserves speech, swallowing and airway defenses and avoids VAP
It gives a larger tidal volume and a guaranteed PaCO₂
It allows deep sedation without loss of airway reflexes
It protects the lower airway from aspiration of gastric contents and secretions
q.e: NPPV lets the patient eat, drink and talk, and avoids artificial-airway complications.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: To minimize gastric insufflation on NIV, inspiratory pressure should stay below what?
q.e: Hess: avoid inspiratory pressure > 20 cm H₂O; RCP 203: IPAP < 20–25.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: Which finding on NIV predicts failure, according to Hess?
q.e: Hess: VT > 10 mL/kg predicts NIV failure; a faster PaCO₂ fall is seen with success.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: What is the most common cause of cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
q.e: Cardiogenic edema is a "pressure problem" from left heart failure backing pressure into the lungs.

q.q: Which sign is classic for cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
o: No sputum and a dry cough only
q.e: Classic signs: pink frothy sputum, tachypnea, PND, orthopnea, crackles.

q.q: Which chest radiograph finding fits cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
o: Cardiomegaly with a bat's-wing pattern and Kerley B lines
Normal heart size with bilateral patchy infiltrates
Hyperlucency with flattened diaphragms and a narrow heart
A single lobar consolidation with air bronchograms
q.e: Cardiomegaly (> 50% of thoracic width), Kerley lines, butterfly opacities, transudative effusion.

q.q: What BNP level is normal?
q.e: BNP < 100 normal; 100–300 suggests HF; > 300 mild; > 600 moderate; > 900 severe.

q.q: What is the management order for cardiogenic pulmonary edema in the deck?
o: Decrease preload → decrease afterload → increase contractility
Increase preload → increase afterload → decrease contractility
Increase preload → decrease afterload → decrease contractility
Decrease afterload → increase preload → increase contractility
q.e: Preload: nitroglycerin, furosemide; afterload: ACE inhibitors, nitroprusside; contractility: dobutamine, milrinone.

q.q: How does CPAP help in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
o: It decreases preload and afterload and reduces shunt
It increases venous return, preload and pulmonary blood volume
It increases shunt and lowers the PaO₂
q.e: ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ preload and afterload, ↑ compliance, ↓ shunt, ↑ PaO₂.

q.q: What CPAP level is best supported for cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
q.e: Hess Ch 21 and the RCP 103 deck: 5–10 cm H₂O; a 10 cm H₂O start fits every range.

q.q: What does the RCP 105 FAQ call the first-line therapy for acute pulmonary edema?
o: Intubation with PEEP of 20 cm H₂O
Nasal cannula at 6 L/min with diuretics
q.e: RCP 105 NIV FAQ: "CPAP 8–12 cmH₂O with 100% oxygen."

q.q: A patient with CHF who is on CPAP develops hypercapnia. Which of the following should be done?
o: Switch to BiPAP with a backup rate
Increase the CPAP to 25 cm H₂O
Lower the FiO₂ and keep the CPAP
q.e: RCP 203: switch to bi-level with a backup rate if hypopnea or hypercapnia appears.

q.q: What normal MAP range does Hess Table 3-1 give?
q.e: Hess: MAP 65–105 mm Hg; the decks give minimums of 60 (tissue) and 70 (cerebral).

q.q: What minimum MAP does the deck give to maintain tissue perfusion?
q.e: MAP 60 for tissue perfusion; MAP 70 for cerebral perfusion pressure.

q.q: Why can NIPPV lower the MAP?
o: Increased intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and cardiac output
Decreased intrathoracic pressure increases venous return and preload
Increased intrathoracic pressure raises the systemic vascular resistance
Increased airway pressure dilates the coronary and cerebral arteries
q.e: ↑ PEEP/EPAP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP.

q.q: What does the leak port on a bilevel circuit do?
o: It serves as the patient's passive exhalation port
It controls the FiO₂ delivered by the oxygen blender
q.e: Bilevel machines use a single-limb circuit; the leak port is the passive exhalation route.

q.q: What is the hazard of a passive leak port if expiratory flow exceeds what it can vent?
q.e: The patient exhales into the hose and rebreathes CO₂; higher EPAP flushes the hose.

q.q: Why is the minimum EPAP on many bilevel ventilators 3–4 cm H₂O?
o: The extra flow it needs flushes exhaled gas from the hose
Lower EPAP raises the delivered FiO₂ above the set value
It prevents oxygen toxicity at high inspiratory pressures
It keeps the mask sealed against the patient's face
q.e: Higher expiratory pressure needs more flow, which flushes the hose and reduces rebreathing.

q.q: What is the most dangerous expiratory obstruction?
o: An obstructed exhalation port on a single-limb NPPV circuit
A kinked inspiratory limb on a dual-limb ICU circuit
A wet heat and moisture exchanger at the wye
A loose temperature probe at the outlet of the heated humidifier chamber
q.e: It can cause rebreathing, asphyxia or barotrauma.

q.q: BiPAP is set at IPAP 15 / EPAP 5. What are the pressure support and PEEP?
q.e: PS = IPAP − EPAP = 10; EPAP = PEEP = 5.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: How does HFNC's pharyngeal pressure differ from PEEP?
o: It is not set; it rises with flow and is lost when the mouth opens
It is set on the machine in cm H₂O, in the same way that PEEP is set
It is fixed at 10 cm H₂O whether the mouth is open or closed
It is set by the FiO₂ and is unaffected by the flow rate
q.e: Pharyngeal pressure rises ~1 cm H₂O per 10 L/min with the mouth closed.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: How does PAP treat obstructive sleep apnea?
o: It acts as a pneumatic splint holding the upper airway open
It stimulates the diaphragm to contract more strongly during sleep
It lowers the PaCO₂ and resets the respiratory drive
It increases the tone of the upper-airway muscles
q.e: Hess: PAP counteracts negative inspiratory pressure and prevents airway collapse.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: How does PEEP affect pulmonary artery pressure (PAP)?
o: It raises it by compressing pulmonary capillaries
It lowers it by dilating pulmonary capillaries
It has no effect on pulmonary vessels
It lowers it by reducing cardiac output
q.e: PPV with PEEP → ↑ PAP from capillary compression and higher PVR.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: A patient on BiPAP has a high PaCO₂. Which of the following should be changed?
o: Decrease IPAP and EPAP by the same amount
q.e: High CO₂ → raise IPAP/PS to increase VT and minute ventilation.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: A BiPAP patient on 10/5 needs better oxygenation but has normal CO₂. What is the NBRC answer?
q.e: Oxygenation only → raise both equally so ΔP stays the same.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: What is the BiPAP rule about raising EPAP?
o: Never raise EPAP without raising IPAP by the same amount
Raise EPAP by itself whenever the PaCO₂ is high and the SpO₂ is normal
Keep EPAP higher than IPAP at all times
Leave EPAP at its starting level throughout
q.e: Raising EPAP alone shrinks PS; pressures change in increments of 2, and PS is never < 4.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: Where is the backup rate set in S/T mode?
o: Two to five breaths below the patient's spontaneous rate
Two to five breaths above the patient's spontaneous rate
Equal to the patient's spontaneous rate
Ten to twelve breaths below the patient's spontaneous rate
q.e: S/T backup rate: 2–5 breaths below the spontaneous RR.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: Which NIV interface would NOT be recommended for BiPAP per the RCP 105 deck?
q.e: Nasal pillows are smallest and most comfortable, but "would NOT be recommended for BiPAP."

q.q: What is the biggest complication of a nasal mask?
q.e: Nasal masks have less aspiration risk and dead space, but leak in mouth-breathers; try a chin strap.

q.q: How tight should NIV headgear be?
o: Loose enough to pass one or two fingers underneath
As tight as possible, to stop all of the mask leak
Tight enough to leave a mark on the bridge of the nose
Loose enough that the mask lifts off with each breath
q.e: Hess: pass one or two fingers under the headgear; pressure sores on the nasal bridge are common.

q.q: What does HiVNI stand for?
q.e: HiVNI = High Velocity Nasal Insufflation (Vapotherm); Airvo is Fisher & Paykel's home HFNC.

q.q: Why does Vapotherm use a small-bore cannula?
o: It gives high velocity and leaves room around the prongs for exhaled gas
It delivers a lower flow and reduces the drying of the nasal mucosa
It seals the nostrils completely and lets the pressure build up
It lowers the FiO₂ and entrains room air around the prongs
q.e: Narrow ID → high velocity; small OD leaves room for egress, flushing CO₂ from dead space.

q.q: Can the Airvo deliver high flow without added oxygen?
o: Yes — heated, humidified room air at high flow
No — it delivers 100% oxygen at every flow
No — it needs a ventilator as its gas source
Yes — but at flows below 10 L/min alone
q.e: High flow is not the same as high O₂; Airvo can give room air or an O₂-enriched mix.

q.q: How does mouthpiece ventilation work during the day?
o: The patient takes assisted breaths from a mouthpiece on a flexible arm as needed
The patient wears a full-face mask and triggers every breath throughout the day
The patient is ventilated through a tracheostomy with a speaking valve
The patient receives timed mandatory breaths by a nasal mask
q.e: Daytime MPV lets the patient talk, eat and stay active; a mask is used at night.

q.q: What does air stacking improve?
o: Inspiratory capacity and peak cough flow
Resting heart rate and blood pressure
q.e: Stacked breaths held with a closed glottis raise IC and peak cough flow and combat atelectasis.

sections.title: Pneumonia (PNA)
sections.covers: 10 items · Signs, symptoms and diagnosis · atypical PNA · Legionella · categories · chlorhexidine

q.q: Which bedside finding fits pneumonia with consolidation?
o: Dull percussion with bronchial breath sounds
Dull percussion with absent breath sounds
q.e: RCP 103: dull over consolidation; crackles, bronchial breath sounds, whispered pectoriloquy.

q.q: How does the pneumonia cough typically change?
o: Starts dry and hacking, then becomes productive
Starts productive, then becomes dry and hacking
Stays dry and hacking for the whole illness
Starts bloody, then becomes dry within a day
q.e: Dry and hacking, then productive (yellow/green), possibly rust-colored or blood-streaked.

q.q: What fever pattern does the RCP 103 deck give for bacterial vs viral pneumonia?
q.e: Bacterial pneumonia > 101 °F; viral < 101 °F.

q.q: Which lab finding is listed in Hess Box 36-1 for pneumonia?
q.e: Lab: leukocytosis, ↑ bands, or leukopenia.

q.q: How is pneumonia diagnosed according to Hess?
o: Clinically — no single test can diagnose it
By a single positive blood culture
By a positive sputum Gram stain and culture alone
q.e: "Pneumonia is a clinical diagnosis... no single test can diagnose pneumonia."

q.q: What does a CBC show in bacterial vs viral pneumonia?
o: ↑ WBC in bacterial; normal or ↓ WBC in viral
↓ WBC in bacterial; ↑ WBC in viral
↑ WBC in bacterial; ↑↑ WBC in viral
Normal WBC in bacterial; ↑ WBC in viral
q.e: RCP 103: ↑ WBC bacterial, ↓ (or normal) WBC viral.

q.q: What is 'the cornerstone' of microbiologic diagnosis of pneumonia?
q.e: Hess: sputum Gram stain and culture; positive ≥ 10⁶ CFU/mL.

q.q: Which ABG pattern is seen early in pneumonia?
o: Respiratory acidosis with a normal PaO₂
Metabolic acidosis with a normal PaO₂
q.e: Early: respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia; severe disease → respiratory acidosis.

q.q: What is procalcitonin mainly used for in pneumonia?
q.e: Procalcitonin rises in bacterial but not viral infection; its main use is stopping antibiotics.

q.q: How is hospital-acquired pneumonia defined?
o: Onset ≥ 48 hours after admission and not incubating at admission
Onset within 24 hours of admission, with a positive culture
Onset in a nursing-home resident within 90 days of admission
Onset ≥ 48 hours after discharge from an acute-care hospital
q.e: HAP = ≥ 48 hours after admission, not present at admission.

q.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
q.e: S. pneumoniae is the most common CAP bacterium.

q.q: For the exam, how is VAP timing defined?
q.e: Use "≥ 48 hours after intubation"; the RCP 105 slide's "within 48 hours" is contradicted by its notes.

q.q: What happened to the HCAP (healthcare-associated pneumonia) category?
o: It was expanded to include all outpatients
It was merged with the VAP category
q.e: Hess: HCAP was retired in 2016 and is no longer separate from HAP.

q.q: Which is the 'most important chronic pneumonia pathogen'?
q.e: TB is the most important chronic pneumonia pathogen, with fungi such as Histoplasma.

q.q: Why is atypical pneumonia called 'atypical'?
o: The organism escapes standard bacteriologic tests; there is no consolidation
The organism affects children alone; there is always lobar consolidation
The organism causes a very high WBC count; the Gram stain is positive
The organism is always acquired in hospital; it resists every antibiotic
q.e: Atypical: escapes standard tests, moderate sputum, no consolidation, only moderate WBC rise.

q.q: What is the most common cause of atypical pneumonia?
q.e: Mycoplasma causes "walking pneumonia," common in crowded settings.

q.q: Why don't penicillins work against Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
o: It is a virus, not a bacterium
q.e: Mycoplasma is the smallest free-living organism and lacks a cell wall.

q.q: What does the RCP 104 deck call the 'go-to' for atypical pneumonia?
q.e: "Atypical pneumonia? → Think macrolide"; doxycycline is also strong atypical coverage.

q.q: What does the chest radiograph typically show in atypical pneumonia?
o: A large unilateral pleural effusion with mediastinal shift
q.e: Typical: lobar consolidation; atypical: diffuse interstitial opacities.

q.q: Where does Legionella pneumophila live?
o: Water systems such as showers, fountains and mist machines
Droppings of birds such as parrots, pigeons and other poultry
Dust from livestock such as sheep and cattle
Soil containing bat or bird droppings
q.e: Legionella colonizes water systems; aerosolized bacteria cause Legionnaires disease.

q.q: Which atypical organism is most likely to lead to ARDS?
q.e: Hess: of the atypical organisms, Legionella is most likely to lead to ARDS.

q.q: What is a limitation of the Legionella urinary antigen test?
q.e: Sensitivity 70–90%, specificity ~99%, but only serogroup 1 — up to 20% test falsely negative.

q.q: Why are ventilator humidifiers filled with sterile water?
o: To keep out heat-resistant organisms such as Legionella
To raise the humidity that the heater can deliver
To prevent condensation from forming in the circuit
To avoid mineral deposits on the temperature probe
q.e: Legionella in hospital tap water has caused epidemic VAP.

q.q: What is first-line treatment for Legionella?
q.e: Hess: fluoroquinolone or macrolide.

q.q: Per the instructor's RCP 203 deck, which oral care is part of the CDC VAP bundle?
o: Weekly oral care with hydrogen peroxide
Daily oral nystatin swish and swallow
Oral care with sterile water once per shift
q.e: Exam answer: daily chlorhexidine oral care (Hess's newer bundle says "no longer recommended").

q.q: What head-of-bed elevation is part of the VAP bundle?
q.e: HOB 30–45° unless contraindicated.

q.q: Which ETT feature helps prevent VAP?
o: Subglottic suction that removes pooled secretions above the cuff
A smaller cuff that is inflated to a higher pressure to seal the trachea
An uncuffed tube that allows secretions to drain
A nasotracheal route that avoids the oropharynx
q.e: Subglottic ETTs continuously remove secretions; use the oral route and avoid nasal intubation.

q.q: What cuff pressure helps prevent VAP?
q.e: Cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O; avoid the minimal leak technique.

q.q: Besides oral care, what is chlorhexidine used for in these sources?
o: Skin antisepsis before an arterial line or thoracentesis
Treating Legionella in hospital water systems
Disinfecting flexible bronchoscopes between one patient and the next
q.e: Scrub the insertion site with chlorhexidine before an arterial line; used before thoracentesis too.

q.q: According to the deck's clinical pearl, what is the single greatest risk factor for VAP?
o: A low PEEP below 5 cm H₂O
q.e: Deck: prolonged MV is the single greatest risk factor; the ETT is the pathway.

q.q: What is the most important bedside finding of VAP?
o: Diminished breath sounds at both bases
q.e: Clinical VAP: fever, leukocytosis/leukopenia, purulent secretions, new infiltrate.

q.q: Which organisms cause late-onset (> 4–5 days) VAP?
q.e: Late-onset or MDR risk: MRSA, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, ESBL organisms.

q.q: What is the primary mechanism of VAP?
o: Microaspiration of secretions pooled above the cuff
Inhalation of contaminated gas from the ventilator circuit
Spread of bacteria to the lungs through the bloodstream
Spread of skin bacteria along the outside of the tube
q.e: The ETT bypasses defenses; microaspiration around the cuff is the primary mechanism.

q.q: How long is the 2016 IDSA/ATS antibiotic course for VAP?
q.e: 7 days for VAP and ≤ 7 days for HAP; de-escalate when cultures return.

q.q: How does aspiration pneumonitis differ from aspiration pneumonia?
o: Pneumonitis is a non-infectious chemical injury from gastric contents
Pneumonitis is a bacterial infection from oral secretions
Pneumonitis is a viral infection after a witnessed aspiration
Pneumonitis is an allergic reaction to inhaled food particles and saliva
q.e: Pneumonitis is chemical (gastric acid); aspiration pneumonia can be toxic, obstructive or infectious.

q.q: Aspiration of gastric fluid with what pH is 'often fatal'?
q.e: RCP 103: aspiration of gastric fluid with pH ≤ 2.5 is often fatal.

q.q: What is Mendelson's syndrome?
o: Tachycardia, dyspnea and cyanosis after acid aspiration, often in pregnancy
Fever, dry cough and headache after exposure to infected bird droppings
Fever, diarrhea and confusion after exposure to contaminated water
Tachycardia, wheezing and rash after an inhaled drug allergy
q.e: Mendelson's syndrome follows acid aspiration, usually in pregnancy.

q.q: Which antibiotic does RCP 104 link with aspiration pneumonia?
q.e: "Aspiration pneumonia → clindamycin" (anaerobic coverage).

q.q: What does CURB-65 stand for?
o: Confusion, BUN ≥ 20, RR ≥ 30, low BP, age ≥ 65
Cyanosis, Urine output, Rate, Blood gas, 65 kg
Crackles, Upper lobe, Radiograph, Breath sounds, 65%
q.e: 1 point each: Confusion, BUN ≥ 20, RR ≥ 30, SBP < 90 or DBP ≤ 60, age ≥ 65.

q.q: A CAP patient has a CURB-65 score of 3. What is the likely disposition?
o: Home oxygen and a clinic visit in 48 hours
q.e: 0–1 outpatient; 2 hospitalization; ≥ 3 hospital and possibly ICU.

q.q: Which of the following is the full group that should receive annual influenza vaccination?
q.e: Hess: annual influenza vaccination for everyone older than 6 months.

q.q: Which pneumococcal vaccines does Hess name?
q.e: PCV13 (13 serotypes) and PPSV23 (23 serotypes).

q.q: What place does pneumonia hold among postoperative complications?
q.e: Pneumonia is the third most common postoperative complication.

q.q: A postoperative patient has atelectasis and a fever. What does the fever suggest?
o: Infection from retained secretions; atelectasis alone does not cause fever
Atelectasis itself, which is the usual cause of a postoperative fever
A normal response to surgery that needs no further assessment
A pulmonary embolism, which is the usual cause of a postoperative fever
q.e: Hess: atelectasis without infection does not result in fever; look for the infection.

q.q: Which lobe is the most common site of clinically significant atelectasis after abdominal surgery?
q.e: Clinically significant atelectasis after abdominal surgery runs 15–20%; LLL is most common.

q.q: What contributes to alveolar collapse during general anesthesia?
q.e: 20–25% of basal lung collapses after induction; FiO₂ > 40% contributes.

sections.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
sections.covers: 6 items · Atelectrauma, biotrauma, pneumotrauma, volutrauma · ALI mortality · who gets ARDS most · why compliance falls

q.q: What is atelectrauma?
o: Injury from repetitive opening and closing of alveoli
Injury from overstretching by too much volume
Injury from too much pressure causing an air leak
Injury from the release of inflammatory cytokines
q.e: Atelectrauma = repetitive collapse and re-opening (shear stress); prevented by PEEP and recruitment.

q.q: What is volutrauma, and how is it prevented?
o: Overstretching from too much volume; prevented by low VT (~6 mL/kg PBW)
Rupture from too much pressure; prevented by high PEEP (~15 cm H₂O)
Collapse of alveoli at end-expiration; prevented by a higher VT
Inflammation from cytokines; prevented by a higher FiO₂
q.e: Deck: "too much volume" overstretches healthy alveoli; "Lower VT → reduce volutrauma."

q.q: On this exam, what does the instructor's term 'pneumotrauma' mean?
o: Barotrauma — rupture and air leak from too much pressure
Biotrauma — cytokine release from ventilator injury
Atelectrauma — repeated opening and closing of alveoli
Volutrauma — overstretching from too much volume
q.e: No source uses "pneumotrauma"; read it as barotrauma (pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema).

q.q: What is biotrauma?
o: The inflammatory cytokine response to ventilator-induced lung injury
The bacterial infection acquired from the ventilator circuit
The rupture of alveoli from excessive airway pressure
The injury to the alveoli that is caused by a high inspired oxygen fraction
q.e: Hess: VILI increases inflammatory cytokines that can spill into the blood and contribute to multiorgan dysfunction.

q.q: How does the deck summarize lung-protective strategy?
o: Low VT prevents overdistention and PEEP prevents collapse — we need both
High VT prevents collapse and zero PEEP prevents overdistention — we need both
High PEEP prevents both collapse and overdistention by itself
Low VT prevents both overdistention and collapse by itself
q.e: "Low VT protects the alveoli from overdistention. PEEP helps prevent them from collapsing. We need both!"

q.q: How was ALI defined by the AECC?
o: P/F less than 300 but greater than 200
P/F less than 200 but greater than 100
P/F less than 400 but greater than 300
P/F less than 100 on any PEEP
q.e: AECC: ALI P/F 201–300; ARDS < 200. The Berlin definition eliminated the term ALI.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: What proportion of ALI/ARDS patients die primarily of refractory hypoxemia?
q.e: Most deaths are from nonpulmonary organ failure; only 10–15% die of refractory hypoxemia.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: In the ARDSnet trial, what was mortality with 6 mL/kg vs 12 mL/kg tidal volumes?
q.e: Low VT (6 mL/kg) reduced mortality to 31% from 40% with 12 mL/kg.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: Where does the majority of ARDS mortality occur?
o: In the setting of sepsis or multisystem organ failure
In the setting of isolated refractory hypoxemia
In the setting of pneumothorax and barotrauma
In the setting of oxygen toxicity from a high FiO₂
q.e: Hess: only ~15% die from respiratory failure; most deaths come with sepsis or MOF.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: Which patients have the highest risk of developing ARDS?
q.e: Hess: sepsis is the highest-risk group (40% incidence); the deck calls it the most common cause.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: Which is a DIRECT (primary) cause of ARDS?
q.e: Direct: pneumonia, aspiration, contusion, inhalation injury. Indirect: sepsis, trauma with shock, transfusion, pancreatitis.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: About what fraction of patients with a witnessed aspiration develop ARDS?
q.e: ARDS deck notes: about one-third of witnessed aspiration events lead to ARDS.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: How soon after the inciting event do ARDS signs typically appear?
q.e: Clinical signs appear 6–72 hours after the insult and progress rapidly.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: What does increased alveolar-capillary permeability in ARDS produce?
q.e: Inflammation → ↑ permeability → protein-rich fluid leaks → noncardiogenic edema.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: Why is surfactant lost in ARDS?
o: Type II cells are damaged and protein-rich edema inactivates surfactant
Type I cells overproduce surfactant, which is then diluted by edema
Type II cells are spared, but high PEEP washes the surfactant out
Oxygen therapy converts surfactant into hyaline membranes
q.e: Type II cell apoptosis/necrosis and protein-rich edema reduce surfactant → atelectasis.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: What are hyaline membranes in ARDS?
o: Fibrin and cellular debris lining the alveolar walls
Layers of healthy surfactant on the alveolar walls
Calcium deposits within the alveolar septa
Mucus plugs lining the small bronchioles
q.e: Hyaline membranes increase stiffness and decrease compliance.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS
